title: Introduction
content:
This chapter introduces the problem, the architecture and the AWS services of shop-ai before you start building. When you finish it you know what you are about to deploy, what each service does and why the team chose it.
Goals Understand the problem of a small shop selling laptops and PC parts, and why a serverless architecture fits. Read the architecture diagram: which services the data goes through in the 3 flows of browsing, ordering and nightly recommendations. Know why each service was chosen and which limitations the team accepted. 5.1.1. The problem A small shop selling laptops and PC parts has nobody to advise “if you buy this, you also need that”: a laptop buyer usually needs a mouse and a bag; a new graphics card often needs a bigger power supply. Customers do not know, so the shop loses cross-sell orders. The shop also has nobody to look after servers, and its traffic is low and uneven: a server running 24/7 sits idle most of the time but is still billed.
Black Magic (the shop-ai project) is a web store that solves this:
The full shopping flow: browse and search products, a cart (also before signing in), cash-on-delivery ordering, viewing and cancelling orders, confirmation emails, an account page and an order administration page. Recommendations from the shop’s own data: “Frequently bought together” on product pages, “For you” from each customer’s history, “Best sellers” when there is not enough data. The model is built by the team and recomputed every night. Fully serverless: no servers to patch or monitor; close to $0 with few visitors, automatic scaling with many. 5.1.2. What you will do in this lab Chapter You will 5.2 Prerequisites Prepare the account, tools, CDK bootstrap, budget alerts and the HMAC key; know what the lab costs 5.3 Deploying the Infrastructure Deploy all of shop-ai to your own sandbox with one CDK command, open the site and sign in 5.4 Sales Flow Orders that are never lost or duplicated: a DynamoDB transaction, Idempotency-Key, SQS, DLQ, SES email 5.5 Recommendations and Data Security Generate data and evaluate the model locally, run the recommendation pipeline on AWS, anonymize user data, run the recommendation poisoning experiment 5.6 Testing and Operations Trace an order with CloudWatch Logs Insights and X-Ray, read alarms and runbooks, handle a real DLQ incident; see the team’s performance numbers 5.7 Clean Up Delete each stack, leftover log groups and keys, check Billing the next day The lab runs in your own sandbox (shop-sbx-<name>) and does not touch the team’s environments. The sandbox has no WAF and no CloudWatch alarms, so it costs close to $0 (details in 5.2).
5.1.3. Architecture The first draft of the diagram was made with AI assistance; the team checked every component, arrow and table read/write permission against the CDK code and corrected it. Everything runs in Singapore (ap-southeast-1), except the CloudFront AWS WAF in us-east-1. The dev, staging and prod environments share one account, and each lab user has their own sandbox.
Browsing and sign-in (steps 1–5)
The customer opens the site over HTTPS through Amazon CloudFront. On prod, AWS WAF filters requests first. Static files come from a private Amazon S3 bucket that only CloudFront can read (OAC). A CloudFront Function handles single-page routes; the product list is cached for 60 seconds. The customer signs up and signs in directly with Amazon Cognito. A Pre sign-up trigger checks the username is unique; a Post confirmation trigger revokes all old sessions after a password reset. Calls to /api/* go to Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API), which checks the Cognito JWT on routes that need sign-in. API Gateway routes to AWS Lambda, one function per module: catalog, cart, account, ordering, ordering-admin, events, recommendation. Ordering (steps 6–9)
The ordering Lambda checks prices, decrements stock, removes items from the cart and writes a PENDING order in one DynamoDB transaction, then sends the order to an Amazon SQS queue. The order-processor worker confirms the order and sends the email through Amazon SES. After 3 failures the message goes to the orders DLQ. The worker publishes order-confirmed to Amazon SNS; an SQS queue receives it so the events-purchase Lambda records an anonymized purchase (events DLQ after 5 failures). Each Lambda reads and writes only the Amazon DynamoDB tables it needs (7 tables). Admin cancellation restores stock in the same transaction. Nightly recommendations (steps 10–11)
At 02:00, Amazon EventBridge Scheduler invokes the recs-pipeline Lambda (Python), which reads the events and products tables, computes the 3 recommendation types, writes a new version to the recs table and only switches the ACTIVE pointer when the quality gate passes. While browsing, the events Lambda records VIEW and ADD_TO_CART with the user ID hashed with HMAC (key in SSM Parameter Store); the recommendation Lambda just reads precomputed results, so pages stay fast. Operations (steps 12–13)
Amazon CloudWatch collects logs, metrics and alarms; AWS X-Ray traces every Lambda; alarms send email through SNS. GitHub Actions deploys with AWS CDK through OIDC, without access keys: a merge to develop goes to dev, a release/* branch to staging, a v* tag to prod after someone else approves. 5.1.4. AWS services and why they were chosen Service Used for Why Amazon CloudFront, AWS WAF Single entry point for web and API; WAF on prod only One domain, caching close to users; WAF blocks bad IPs, rate-limits, applies the AWS common rule set (ADR-0006) Amazon S3 Static web (React) Cheap, readable only by CloudFront through OAC Amazon Cognito Sign-up, sign-in, admin group No self-stored passwords; issues JWTs for the API (ADR-0007) Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) API routing, JWT check Cheaper than REST API, built-in JWT authorizer (ADR-0007) AWS Lambda Business logic, worker, recommendation job Pay per invocation, scales automatically; outside a VPC so there is no NAT Gateway cost (ADR-0005) Amazon DynamoDB Products, carts, orders, events, recommendations On-demand, serverless, one table per module to limit permissions (ADR-0012); PITR for recovery Amazon SQS, Amazon SNS Asynchronous ordering, purchase events for recommendations Ordering answers fast; a failing worker does not lose orders thanks to the DLQ Amazon SES Confirmation and cancellation emails Sends email from Lambda, billed per message Amazon EventBridge Scheduler Runs the recommendation job at 02:00 A schedule without servers AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store HMAC key Encrypted secret, not in the code Amazon CloudWatch, AWS X-Ray Logs, metrics, alarms, traces Monitoring and alerting, each alarm with a runbook AWS CDK, GitHub Actions (OIDC) Infrastructure as code, automated deployment Rebuild a whole environment with one command; no long-lived access keys (ADR-0008) Own recommendation model instead of Amazon Personalize: following the mentor’s feedback (01/10/2026), the team built its own model on Lambda and DynamoDB so every step can be understood and explained (ADR-0016). The pipeline uses association rules for “frequently bought together”, item-based collaborative filtering for “for you”, and best sellers as the fallback.
5.1.5. Known limitations The team accepted and documented these limitations; you will meet them again in later chapters:
Calling the execute-api URL of API Gateway directly bypasses WAF (C1 on the diagram); stage throttling and JWT checks still apply. SES is still in sandbox: emails only reach verified addresses. An old access token keeps working until it expires (at most 1 hour) after sessions are revoked.

title: Prerequisites
content:
This chapter prepares everything you need before deploying shop-ai: an AWS account, the tools on your machine, the source code, CDK bootstrap, budget alerts and the HMAC key. It ends with the expected cost, estimated with AWS Pricing Calculator and compared with the team’s real bill.
Goals Your machine has the right tool versions and can sign in to AWS from the CLI. Your AWS account is CDK-bootstrapped in ap-southeast-1 and has budgets that email you when spending passes a threshold. An HMAC key exists in Parameter Store, so recommendations work right after the deploy. You know how much this lab costs, and how much a month of real use costs. 5.2.1. AWS account An AWS account. Use a separate account for the lab, not one that runs real workloads. An IAM user or role with administrator access (AdministratorAccess). CDK creates IAM roles, CloudFormation stacks, Lambda, DynamoDB, S3, CloudFront, Cognito, SQS and SNS. Lab Region: Asia Pacific (Singapore) ap-southeast-1. Do not use the root user for the lab, and do not create long-term access keys. Step 5.2.3 signs in with aws login, which gives temporary credentials.
5.2.2. Install the tools Tool Version Check Git any git --version Node.js 24 (set in the repo’s .nvmrc) node --version pnpm 12 (the repo pins pnpm@12.8.1) pnpm --version AWS CLI v2, a version that has aws login aws --version Install pnpm after Node.js:
npm install -g pnpm@12 You do not need to install AWS CDK separately: the CDK CLI version is pinned in infra/package.json and always runs through pnpm --filter infra exec cdk. Docker is not needed either: TypeScript Lambdas are bundled with esbuild, and the Python Lambda only needs its files copied.
Get the source code and install dependencies:
git clone https://github.com/hhieuann/shop-ai.git cd shop-ai git checkout develop pnpm install 5.2.3. Sign in to AWS from your machine aws login The command opens a browser to sign in, then stores temporary credentials for the CLI. They expire after a few hours; when an AWS command says they expired, run aws login again.
Check that you are in the right account and set the default Region:
aws sts get-caller-identity --query Arn --output text aws configure set region ap-southeast-1 5.2.4. Bootstrap CDK CDK needs a CDKToolkit stack (a bucket for Lambda code and the deploy roles) in every Region it deploys to. The sandbox only uses ap-southeast-1. Run this in PowerShell from the repo root:
$acct = aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text; pnpm --filter infra exec cdk bootstrap "aws://$acct/ap-southeast-1" It ends with Environment aws://…/ap-southeast-1 bootstrapped. You only do this once per account.
The team’s prod environment also has AWS WAF. A web ACL attached to CloudFront must live in us-east-1, so the team’s account is bootstrapped in both Regions. The lab sandbox has no WAF, so skip us-east-1.
5.2.5. Create budget alerts Create budgets before deploying, so a forgotten resource sends you an email.
Open Billing and Cost Management → Budgets → Create budget. Choose Use a template → Monthly cost budget. Set Budgeted amount to 5, enter the email address for alerts, then Create budget. Repeat with 10 and 20 if you want several levels. AWS emails you when actual cost passes 85% and 100% of the amount, and when forecasted cost passes 100%. The team uses exactly these three budgets ($5, $10, $20) on the project account.
5.2.6. Create the HMAC key for behaviour data shop-ai does not store real userId values in the events table used for recommendations. A Lambda hashes userId with HMAC-SHA256 and a secret key stored in SSM Parameter Store at /shop/<environment>/events/hmac-key. The key is not in CDK (no secrets in source code), so you create it once by hand before deploying. The sandbox uses the sbx environment.
Check whether the key exists:
aws ssm describe-parameters --region ap-southeast-1 --parameter-filters "Key=Name,Values=/shop/sbx/events/hmac-key" --query "Parameters[].Name" --output text If the output is empty, create a random 32-byte key. The command does not print the key and clears the variable afterwards (PowerShell):
$k = [Convert]::ToBase64String([System.Security.Cryptography.RandomNumberGenerator]::GetBytes(32)); aws ssm put-parameter --region ap-southeast-1 --name /shop/sbx/events/hmac-key --type SecureString --value $k --query Version --output text; Remove-Variable k It prints 1 (the first version of the parameter).
Do not change the key on a running environment: the same user would hash to a different value and their past behaviour would no longer match. If you skip this step, ordering still works but the purchase event messages end up in a DLQ. Chapter 5.6.5 describes exactly this incident and how to fix it.
5.2.7. Cost How much does this lab cost? Close to $0. The lab sandbox has no WAF and creates no CloudWatch alarms (the two biggest costs in prod). Every other service is billed per use, and one person’s lab traffic fits within the Free Tier. Remember to do chapter 5.7 to delete the resources when you finish.
How much does a month of real use cost? The team built an estimate in AWS Pricing Calculator for “a small shop running in prod for one month”, using the configuration in the CDK code:
Estimate link: https://calculator.aws/#/estimate?id=0798eb584d82c280a557b96fbf3c8fbe695a6ca0
Traffic assumptions:
Assumption Value How Visits 30,000/month about 1,000 a day API requests 450,000/month 15 requests per visit: products, recommendations, cart, events CloudFront requests 1,050,000/month 35 requests per visit (API plus static files) Data out from CloudFront 50 GB/month about 1.5 MB per visit Orders, emails 300 orders, 600 emails confirmation and cancellation emails Signed-in users 2,000 MAU Result (Singapore, before tax):
Service Main configuration USD/month AWS WAF 1 web ACL, 2 rate-based rules + 3 managed rule groups, 1.05 million requests 10.63 Amazon CloudFront 50 GB out to the internet, 1.05 million HTTPS requests 7.32 Amazon CloudWatch 1 GB of logs (kept 2 weeks), 10 alarms, 1 dashboard, 5 custom metrics 3.21 AWS X-Ray 460,000 traces 2.34 Amazon DynamoDB On-demand, 0.2 million writes, 0.9 million reads, PITR 0.71 Amazon API Gateway HTTP API, 450,000 requests 0.56 Amazon SES 600 emails 0.06 Amazon S3 0.1 GB, 21,000 requests 0.02 Amazon Cognito Lite plan, 2,000 MAU 0.01 AWS Lambda Arm, 512 MB, 460,000 invocations, 150 ms 0.00 Amazon SQS, SNS, EventBridge Scheduler, SSM Parameter Store 0.00 Total 24.86 (298.32/year) The Calculator does not subtract the CloudFront Free Tier (1 TB and 10 million requests a month). At 50 GB and 1.05 million requests, the $7.32 is really $0. So the real cost is about $17.5/month, more than half of it WAF. There is no VPC, NAT gateway, EC2, RDS or load balancer, so there are no other fixed costs.
If you build the estimate yourself, watch out for three defaults that distort the result:
DynamoDB defaults to provisioned capacity (about $30/month plus $205 upfront). Turn it off and turn on on-demand capacity. Cognito defaults to Advanced security features on (about $100/month at 2,000 MAU). shop-ai does not use them; choose Disabled. SNS and EventBridge Scheduler default to “million per month”, and the fields do not accept decimals. Change the unit to “per month”, then enter 300 and 30. Compared with the real bill Cost Explorer for the team’s account, 01–15/11/2026, covering dev, staging and prod, before credits:
Service Real cost AWS WAF $1.27 (WAF on since 12/11, about $0.33/day, or about $10/month) AWS Cost Explorer $0.07 (Cost Explorer API calls) Amazon DynamoDB $0.07 Amazon API Gateway $0.04 Amazon S3 $0.02 Amazon SES, CloudFront under $0.01 Lambda, Cognito, SQS, SNS, CloudWatch, X-Ray $0 (within the Free Tier) The real numbers match the estimate: at demo traffic, WAF is almost the whole bill. The serverless services cost close to $0 because they are billed per use. The second item to watch is CloudWatch alarms: the three environments have 13 alarms, counted as 20 metrics (an alarm with metric math counts as 2), which is above the 10 free alarms and costs about $1/month. The team will remove WAF after the submission, following the runbook docs/runbooks/waf.md.
Preparation is done. Chapter 5.3 deploys the shop-ai infrastructure to your sandbox with CDK.

title: Proposal
content:
Black Magic: a PC parts store with product recommendations, serverless on AWS Team shop-ai: Nguyễn Hiếu An (team lead), Nguyễn Minh Hoàng, Nguyễn Trọng Nhân. FCAJ program, OJT from 14/09/2026.
Source code: github.com/hhieuann/shop-ai
1. Summary Small PC parts shops have nobody to advise “if you buy this, you also need that”, so they lose cross-sell revenue. The team built Black Magic, a store whose recommendations learn from the shop’s own purchase data, running fully serverless on AWS: no servers to look after, close to zero cost with few visitors, and automatic scaling when traffic grows.
The system covers the full shopping flow (browsing, cart, ordering, account, order administration), 3 kinds of recommendations (frequently bought together, for you, best sellers), security from the start, 3 environments dev, staging, prod, and automated deployment. Version v1.0.0 went to prod on 23/11/2026. The estimated cost for real use is about $24.86/month.
2. Problem A customer buying a laptop usually needs a mouse and a bag; a graphics card often needs a bigger power supply. Customers do not know, small shops lack staff to advise, so cross-sell orders are lost. Big marketplaces have recommendation engines, small shops do not: running servers and a recommender costs money and needs an operator. Small shops have low, uneven traffic. A server running 24/7 sits idle most of the time but still costs money. 3. Solution A web store built on pay-per-use AWS services, with recommendations recomputed every night from the shop’s own data.
What users can do:
Customers: browse and search by category, add to cart (even before signing in), order with cash on delivery (COD), view and cancel orders, receive confirmation emails; manage their account (change username, change password, forgot password). Recommendations: “Frequently bought together” on product pages, “For you” based on each customer’s history, “Best sellers” when there is not enough data. Admin: view orders by status, move orders to shipping and delivered, cancel orders (stock is restored). Recommender: following the mentor’s feedback (01/10/2026), the team does not use Amazon Personalize and builds its own model on Lambda and DynamoDB (ADR-0016), so every step can be understood and explained. Each night a Python job computes:
frequently bought together with association rules (counting items often bought together); for you with item-based collaborative filtering; best sellers as the fallback. Results are only switched on after passing a quality gate; behaviour data hashes user IDs (HMAC) and expires after 90 days.
Out of scope (future work): online payment, part compatibility checks, complex inventory, returns, a mobile app, a shopping assistant using Amazon Bedrock.
4. Architecture Everything runs in Singapore (ap-southeast-1), except the CloudFront AWS WAF in us-east-1.
The first draft of the diagram was made with AI assistance; the team checked every component, arrow and table read/write permission against the CDK code and corrected it.
Need AWS service Why Single entry point, static web Amazon CloudFront, Amazon S3 (OAC) Close to users, caches the product API; only CloudFront can read S3 Block bad traffic (prod only) AWS WAF IP reputation list, rate limits, AWS common rule set Sign-in, roles Amazon Cognito No self-stored passwords; the API checks JWTs API Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) Cheap, built-in JWT check Business logic AWS Lambda (one function per module) Pay per invocation, scales automatically Data Amazon DynamoDB (on-demand, PITR) Serverless, one table per module, point-in-time recovery Asynchronous ordering Amazon SQS (with DLQ), Amazon SNS Ordering answers fast, processing happens later, failures do not lose orders Email Amazon SES Order confirmation and cancellation emails Nightly recommendation job Amazon EventBridge Scheduler, Python Lambda Runs at 02:00, no server needed Secrets AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store HMAC key for behaviour data Monitoring Amazon CloudWatch, AWS X-Ray Alarms by email, each with a runbook Infrastructure, deployment AWS CDK, GitHub Actions (OIDC) Infrastructure as code; deploys without access keys Three main flows:
Browsing: CloudFront → API Gateway → catalog Lambda, recommendation Lambda (reads precomputed recommendations) and events Lambda (records views and add-to-cart). Ordering: the ordering Lambda checks prices, decrements stock, removes items from the cart and writes the order in one DynamoDB transaction, then sends to SQS. A worker confirms the order, sends the SES email and publishes to SNS to record the purchase for recommendations. After 3 failures the message goes to the DLQ. Nightly recommendations: EventBridge Scheduler invokes a Python Lambda that reads the events and products tables, computes the 3 kinds of recommendations and switches to the new version if it passes the gate. 5. Security A single entry point through CloudFront; prod has a WAF blocking with the AWS common rule set (checked: queries with <script> or ../etc/passwd get 403). Security headers at CloudFront (CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options…); OWASP ZAP scan of dev: 0 FAIL. Least-privilege IAM for every Lambda; cdk-nag checks on every synth. Deploys from GitHub Actions through OIDC, no long-lived access keys. Resetting or changing a password revokes all old sessions (Cognito does not do this by itself). A threat model with 14 entries for accounts plus ordering, events and infrastructure; each entry has a mitigation and a status. 6. Plan and progress Two-week sprints, git-flow (develop, release/*, main); every PR has CI (lint, tests, build, cdk-nag, security scans) and a reviewer.
Milestone Date Content Kick-off 14/09–30/09/2026 Problem, product category, architecture; account, budgets; CDK skeleton, CI/CD Recommender change 01/10/2026 Dropped Amazon Personalize, built our own model (ADR-0016) v0.1.0 22/10/2026 Browsing, search, accounts, cart; CloudFront, monitoring, E2E v0.2.0 05/11/2026 Asynchronous ordering, SES email, event tracking, nightly recommendations, recommendation blocks on the web v1.0.0-rc.1 11/11/2026 Prod WAF, admin order status, new product page, performance measurements, recovery drill v1.0.0 23/11/2026 Account page, forgot/change password, admin cancellation; prod WAF blocking Report submission about 29/11/2026 Workshop, blogs, demo video Roles:
Member Main responsibilities Nguyễn Hiếu An Team lead; CDK infrastructure, CI/CD, security, monitoring, cost; recommendation API; release coordination Nguyễn Minh Hoàng Web (React), ordering, cart, account, admin, two-factor authentication Nguyễn Trọng Nhân Data and the recommendation pipeline, threat model, WAF, recommendation poisoning experiment 7. Cost AWS Pricing Calculator estimate for a small shop running for real for 1 month (about 1,000 visits/day, 300 orders, 2,000 signed-in users): $24.86/month (estimate). Details in chapter 5.2.
Service USD/month AWS WAF 10.63 Amazon CloudFront 7.32 (actually $0 within the Free Tier, which the Calculator does not subtract) Amazon CloudWatch 3.21 AWS X-Ray 2.34 DynamoDB, API Gateway, SES, S3, Cognito, Lambda, SQS, SNS, Scheduler 1.36 Total 24.86 The real bill for 01–15/11/2026 (all 3 environments) matches the estimate: WAF is almost the whole cost, serverless services are close to $0. The account has 3 budget alerts at $5, $10 and $20.
8. Risks and mitigations Risk Level Mitigation Unexpected AWS bill Medium 3 budget alerts; no NAT, EC2 or RDS; remove unused environments; remove the WAF after submission Poor recommendations with little data Medium Quality gate; best-seller fallback; synthetic data based on personas Attackers spamming events to push recommendations Low WAF rate limits; the experiment showed only 0.3–2% weight shift Data loss from accidental deletion Low PITR; recovery drill done on staging Email only reaches verified addresses Low SES still in sandbox, listed as a known limitation; orders are processed normally Missing deadlines with a small team Medium Many small releases, a checklist for each, cross acceptance testing (testers are not authors) 9. Results Metric Target Result Mobile page performance (Lighthouse) ≥ 90 94–99 Read API p95 (k6, 200 virtual users) ≤ 300 ms 108 ms, 0 errors Ordering p95 ≤ 800 ms 269 ms Data recovery (PITR) lose at most 5 minutes, recover within 1 hour met, new table ready in 3–10 minutes v1.0.0 acceptance on staging all cases pass 8/8 passed v1.0.0 has run on prod since 23/11/2026, with automated deploy and smoke tests green.

title: Week 2 Worklog
content:
Week 2 Objectives: Practice VPC: the network foundation for every later lab and for the workshop. Prepare the next Module 1 labs: EC2, IAM Roles for EC2, S3. Choose a lab path aligned with the fullstack developer direction. Start looking for a workshop topic for the team. Tasks to be carried out this week: Day Task Start Date Completion Date Reference Material 2 - Self-study on AWS Skill Builder, AWS Cloud Practitioner Essentials, Module 4 - Going Global: Regions, Availability Zones, edge locations and Amazon CloudFront, ways to provision AWS resources 21/09/2026 21/09/2026 https://skillbuilder.aws/learn/94T2BEN85A/aws-cloud-practitioner-essentials/ 3 - Practice lab 000003 VPC in the Singapore region (ap-southeast-1):

title: Deploying the Infrastructure
content:
This chapter deploys all of shop-ai to your sandbox with AWS CDK: one command creates the DynamoDB tables, Lambda functions, HTTP API, Cognito, queues, S3 bucket and CloudFront. You then open the web app, sign up, and check the security headers that CloudFront adds. The last two sections are further reading about things that exist only in the team’s environments: AWS WAF in prod, and CI/CD with GitHub Actions without access keys.
Goals Deploy the two stacks shop-sbx-<name>-api and shop-sbx-<name>-web. Open the web app through CloudFront, see the demo products, sign up and sign in. Understand how CloudFront splits requests between S3 and API Gateway, and which security headers it adds. Finish chapter 5.2 first: you have run aws login, bootstrapped CDK and created the HMAC key.
5.3.1. Choose a sandbox name Everyone has their own sandbox, identified by a short name made of lowercase letters and digits only (for example an, hoang). The name becomes the prefix of every stack: shop-sbx-<name>-api, shop-sbx-<name>-web. The commands below use an; replace it with your own name.
Every CDK command must include -c env=..., and a sandbox also needs -c owner=.... If either is missing, CDK stops immediately, so nobody deploys to dev, staging or prod by mistake.
5.3.2. Build the web app The web stack uploads apps/web/dist to S3, so build it first. From the repo root:
pnpm --filter web build If you forget, every CDK command stops with a message asking you to run pnpm --filter web build before synth or deploy.
5.3.3. Preview the changes pnpm --filter infra exec cdk diff --all -c env=sbx -c owner=an The command lists every resource that will be created; on the first run every line has [+]. Every synth also runs cdk-nag against the AWS Solutions rules. If a finding has no recorded justification, synth fails before anything is deployed.
The CDK app has two stacks:
Stack Contains Notes shop-sbx-an-api 7 DynamoDB tables, about 13 Lambda functions (Node.js 24, arm64), an HTTP API with a JWT authorizer, a Cognito user pool, SQS and DLQs, SNS, EventBridge Scheduler A custom resource SeedProducts loads 104 demo products into the products table shop-sbx-an-web An S3 bucket (public access blocked), CloudFront with Origin Access Control, a response headers policy, a config.json file Depends on the api stack: it needs the API URL and the user pool IDs 5.3.4. Deploy pnpm --filter infra exec cdk deploy --all -c env=sbx -c owner=an CDK shows the IAM permissions it will create and asks Do you wish to deploy these changes (y/n)?. Type y. The api stack deploys first, then the web stack, about 5 minutes in total; CloudFront alone takes a few minutes to push its configuration to the edge locations.
When it finishes, CDK prints the outputs. The two you need:
Outputs: shop-sbx-an-api.ApiUrl = https://xxxxxxxxxx.execute-api.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com shop-sbx-an-web.WebUrl = https://dxxxxxxxxxxxxx.cloudfront.net Check in the console: CloudFormation → Stacks, type shop-sbx in the filter. Both stacks must be CREATE_COMPLETE.
To see the outputs later: CloudFormation → select the stack → Outputs tab. That tab also shows ARNs and queue URLs that contain your account ID, so hide them before sharing a screenshot.
5.3.5. Open the web app, sign up and sign in Open WebUrl in a browser. The home page shows the categories; Tất cả sản phẩm (All products) lists the 104 demo products that were just loaded.
Click Đăng ký (Sign up) and fill in Username, Email, Password (at least 8 characters) and Confirm password. Use an email address you can read: Cognito sends a verification code to it.
Enter the code, then sign in with the email and password you just created.
The web app has no Cognito settings built in. On load it reads /config.json (the web stack creates this file from the api stack’s outputs), then talks directly to Cognito using SRP: the password never passes through CloudFront or the API. The tokens it receives go with every API request, and API Gateway’s JWT authorizer checks them before calling a Lambda.
Cognito sends verification emails from the default AWS address, limited to about 50 emails a day per account, which is enough for the lab. Order confirmation emails are sent by SES, which the sandbox turns off (see the note in chapter 5.6.1).
5.3.6. CloudFront: one domain for the web app and the API The CloudFront distribution has three behaviors, matched in order:
Path Goes to Cache /api/v1/products* API Gateway 60 seconds, keyed by query string. The product list is the most called API /api/* API Gateway None. Cart, orders and events are per-user data default S3 (through Origin Access Control) Optimised for static files The web app and the API share one domain, so the browser does not need CORS. The S3 bucket blocks all public access; only this distribution can read it, through Origin Access Control.
Check the routing (replace with your WebUrl):
curl -s "https://dxxxxxxxxxxxxx.cloudfront.net/api/v1/products?limit=1" curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://dxxxxxxxxxxxxx.cloudfront.net/api/v1/me The first returns JSON with one product. The second returns 401: /me requires sign-in, and the JWT authorizer rejected a request without a token.
5.3.7. Security headers Every response from CloudFront goes through a response headers policy. See the real headers with:
curl -sI https://dxxxxxxxxxxxxx.cloudfront.net/ Result on the team’s sandbox (16/11/2026), unrelated lines removed:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK X-Frame-Options: DENY Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data: https:; font-src 'self'; connect-src 'self' https://cognito-idp.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'; form-action 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none' X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(), payment=() Header Effect Content-Security-Policy The browser only runs scripts and styles from this domain, with no 'unsafe-inline', so a script injected into the page (XSS) does not run. connect-src allows Cognito because the web app signs in directly with Cognito Strict-Transport-Security The browser uses only HTTPS for this site for one year. CloudFront also redirects http:// to https:// X-Frame-Options: DENY, frame-ancestors 'none' No site can embed the shop in an iframe, which prevents clickjacking X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff The browser does not guess file types Referrer-Policy Only the domain, not the full path, is sent when a user follows a link to another site Permissions-Policy Turns off camera, microphone, location and payment, which the shop does not use Adding these headers cut the OWASP ZAP scan from 12 warnings to 6 (chapter 5.6.6).
5.3.8. Further reading: AWS WAF in prod The sandbox, dev and staging have no WAF, to save money (a web ACL costs about $10/month, see 5.2.7). In prod a web ACL is attached to CloudFront with five rules, in order:
Priority Rule What it does 10 AWSManagedRulesAmazonIpReputationList Blocks IPs on AWS’s reputation list (bots, known attack sources) 20 RateLimitPerIp Blocks an IP that sends more than 1,000 requests in 5 minutes 30 RateLimitEventsPerIp For /api/v1/events only: more than 300 requests in 5 minutes is blocked, so nobody can flood fake events to skew recommendations 40 AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet General rules: XSS, path traversal, unusual request sizes 50 AWSManagedRulesKnownBadInputsRuleSet Known attack patterns such as Log4Shell A web ACL for CloudFront must live in us-east-1, so WAF is a separate stack (shop-prd-waf) in that Region. CDK passes the web ACL ARN to the web stack with crossRegionReferences. WAF logs go to CloudWatch Logs, log group aws-waf-logs-shop-prd, kept for 14 days.
The common rule set can block legitimate requests, so the team first ran it in count mode. From the v1.0.0-rc.1 deploy (12/11) to 16/11 the logs had 678 requests and 0 blocks. The common rule set counted 74 requests, all of them the team’s own XSS test requests; no real request was wrongly matched. From v1.0.0 the rule set blocks.
5.3.9. Further reading: CI/CD with GitHub Actions and no access keys You deploy your sandbox from your own machine. The shared environments (dev, staging, prod) are deployed only by GitHub Actions:
Event Environment Condition Merge into develop dev automatic Push a release/* branch staging automatic Push a vX.Y.Z tag prod another team member must approve (GitHub environment production) After each deploy the workflow runs smoke tests, plus end-to-end tests on dev and staging.
GitHub stores no AWS access keys. Instead:
The job asks GitHub for an OIDC token signed for that run only. The job calls sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity with the token and gets temporary credentials that last about an hour. The role’s trust policy matches the token’s sub field against the repository and GitHub environment. A job in the dev environment can only assume gh-deploy-dev; to use gh-deploy-prod the job must run in the production environment, which means someone approved it. A job running on a pull request can only assume gh-diff-readonly to run cdk diff, with no write access. The OIDC provider and the four roles are in infra/bootstrap/github-oidc.yaml, deployed once per account. One problem worth recording: GitHub repositories created after July 2026 use a new sub format that contains immutable IDs of the owner and the repository (repo:<owner>@<id>/<repo>@<id>:environment:dev), so a trust policy written for the old format fails with Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. The fix came from reading the real sub value in the CloudTrail AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity event.
The infrastructure is running. Chapter 5.4 walks through the sales flow: cart, ordering through SQS and confirmation emails.

title: Blogs Posted
content:
The three shared blog posts of the shop-ai team, posted on the AWS Study Group Facebook group (by the program rules each team has 3 shared posts). The posts are written in Vietnamese.
Blog 1: GitHub Actions to AWS with OIDC Author: Nguyễn Hiếu An
Title: 🔐 GitHub Actions vào AWS bằng OIDC (GitHub Actions to AWS with OIDC: granting access without storing long-lived access keys)
Content: Why a CI/CD workflow needs an identity on AWS, the risk of long-lived access keys stored in GitHub Secrets, and how OIDC lets the workflow get temporary credentials: GitHub issues a token, AWS STS checks the trust policy (repository, branch, environment) and returns the role’s credentials. Explains aud and sub, setting up the provider and role, and the common error when sub does not match.
Link: https://www.facebook.com/groups/awsstudygroupfcj/permalink/2325503738214585/
Blog 2: A DynamoDB PITR restore drill Author: Nguyễn Hiếu An
Title: 🛟 Bật PITR rồi, bạn đã thử khôi phục bảng DynamoDB chưa? (PITR is on, but have you tried restoring a DynamoDB table?)
Content: RPO and RTO; Point-in-Time Recovery always restores to a new table; real numbers from the 09/11/2026 drill on staging (23 = 23 items, a ~9 KB table still took 3–10 minutes, the latest restorable time was 4 min 59 s behind). Three lessons: the table-exists waiter only waits about 8 minutes; the new table does not carry over TTL, PITR, deletion protection or tags; pointing the application at the new table runs into IAM and IaC ownership. States clearly what was not drilled (copying data back, full RTO).
Link: https://www.facebook.com/groups/awsstudygroupfcj/posts/2334688377296121/
Blog 3: Amazon Cognito and Lambda triggers for user accounts Author: Nguyễn Minh Hoàng (posted 18/11/2026)
Title: 🔑 Đổi mật khẩu rồi mà điện thoại kia vẫn đăng nhập? Kinh nghiệm dùng Amazon Cognito và Lambda trigger (Changed the password but the other phone is still signed in? Lessons from Amazon Cognito and Lambda triggers)
Content: A Cognito User Pool handles the hard parts of accounts (password storage, verification codes, lockout after repeated failures, JWTs), while shop-specific rules need Lambda triggers. The Pre sign-up trigger that checks duplicate usernames timed out on cold starts: Cognito waits at most 5 seconds for a trigger, so the team raised memory to 512 MB and set the timeout to exactly 5 seconds; the alarm had to separate real errors from rule-based rejections. Triggers do not guard every door (calling Cognito’s API directly bypasses them). Forgot password: user-existence protection, no “check the code only” call, the default email sender’s ~50 emails/day. Cognito resets the password but does not sign out other devices, so the team added a Post confirmation trigger calling global sign-out; the catches are that the trigger runs after the password is already changed, and old access tokens keep working until they expire.
Link: https://www.facebook.com/groups/awsstudygroupfcj/posts/2342420569856235/

title: Sales Flow
content:
This chapter walks you through rebuilding the shop-ai sales flow: adding to the cart, placing an order with an Idempotency-Key, the order travelling through an SQS queue to a worker that confirms it and sends an SES email, cancelling an order to restock, and an admin moving the order through delivery. It focuses on two questions: can an order be lost when part of the system fails, and does clicking “place order” twice create two orders. Finish 5.1 Introduction, 5.2 Prerequisite and 5.3 Infrastructure first: the sandbox stacks shop-sbx-<name>-api and shop-sbx-<name>-web must be deployed to your account. In this chapter <name> is the value you used in -c owner=<name> when deploying.
Goals After this chapter you will:
Understand the path of one order: web → API Gateway → ordering Lambda → DynamoDB (one transaction) → SQS → worker Lambda → SES and SNS. See why stock is never decremented wrongly: decrementing stock, writing the order and removing the items from the cart happen in one TransactWriteItems, and every stock decrement has the condition stock >= quantity. Try Idempotency-Key: resending the same key returns the same order, never a second one. Pause the worker, then resume it, and see the order wait in the queue instead of being lost. Cancel an order and see stock added back exactly once, and move an order through delivery with an admin account. 5.4.1. Sales flow architecture Figure 01. Sales flow diagram with numbered flows 1–7: (1) Cognito sign-in; (2) API call through CloudFront; (3) cart; (4) place order; (5) process order; (6) 3 failures to the DLQ; (7) admin. Path: Web (CloudFront) → API Gateway (Cognito JWT) → ordering Lambda → DynamoDB products, carts, orders, order-idempotency (one transaction) → SQS orders queue (DLQ after 3 failures) → order-processor Lambda → SES (customer email) and SNS order-confirmed → the events module’s SQS queue; the admin Lambda reads the byStatus index of orders. Open the interactive diagram: press a flow to walk its arrows in order, click a component to read its role. Drawn with the AWSketch skill from a JSON spec.
Component Purpose Notable settings (infra/lib/api-stack.ts) carts table One cart per customer (key userId), the item list in one item On-demand; conditional writes on version so two tabs editing the cart don’t overwrite each other orders table Orders (key userId + orderId, a ULID) byStatus index for admin; the same table holds a #OPEN counter item (at most 3 open orders) and a #KEY#<Idempotency-Key> marker item with TTL expiresAt; point-in-time recovery on order-idempotency table Powertools Idempotency records against double processing Key id, TTL expiration (24 hours) ordering Lambda POST/GET /api/v1/orders, GET/DELETE /api/v1/orders/{orderId} 512 MB, 10 s timeout, may write only the tables it needs Orders queue (SQS) New and cancelled orders waiting for the worker SQS-managed encryption, TLS only, 60 s visibility timeout, after 3 failures a message moves to the DLQ (kept 14 days) order-processor Lambda (worker) Confirms orders, sends emails, publishes order-confirmed 256 MB, 10 s timeout, up to 5 messages per batch, reports failures per message (reportBatchItemFailures), at most 2 concurrent instances (to pace SES sandbox) Admin Lambda GET/PATCH/DELETE /api/v1/admin/orders… Only the Cognito admin group may call it (checked in the backend, 403 otherwise) Order state machine (docs/business/ordering.md):
PENDING ──► CONFIRMED ──► SHIPPED ──► DELIVERED │ │ │ └────────────┴────────────┴──► CANCELLED (restock) The API sets PENDING, the worker sets CONFIRMED, the admin sets SHIPPED and DELIVERED. Customers can cancel in PENDING or CONFIRMED; admins can also cancel in SHIPPED.
5.4.2. Preparation 5.2 Prerequisite done (AWS CLI, Node, pnpm, shop-ai repo) and 5.3 done (both sandbox stacks deployed). An account registered on your web app (URL in the WebUrl output of shop-sbx-<name>-web). jq to read JSON in the commands below (Git Bash on Windows: download jq from its official site and add it to PATH). Read the API stack outputs you need: STACK=shop-sbx-<name>-api aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name "$STACK" \ --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='ApiUrl' || OutputKey=='OrdersTableName' || OutputKey=='OrdersQueueUrl' || OutputKey=='UserPoolId' || OutputKey=='UserPoolE2eClientId'].[OutputKey,OutputValue]" \ --output text \ | sed -E 's/[0-9]{12}/<account-id>/g; s/(ap-southeast-1_)[A-Za-z0-9]+/\1xxxxxxxx/g' \ | awk -F'\t' '{printf "%-21s %s\n", $1, $2}' Figure 02. The API stack outputs; the command replaced the account ID with <account-id> and masked the user pool ID.
Turn on SES email for the worker The worker sends email only when the deploy passes a sender address (-c senderEmail); without it the worker skips the email step and everything else still runs. A new SES account is in the sandbox: it can send only to verified addresses, at most 1 email per second. For this lab, the simplest setup is to use the same address as the sender and as the email of your web account.
Verify the address (not done in CDK because the identity is account-wide; deleting the stack would remove it):
aws sesv2 create-email-identity --email-identity <your email> --region ap-southeast-1 Open your inbox and click the AWS verification link.
Console → Amazon SES → Identities: the address shows Verified.
Build the web app and redeploy the API stack with the sender address:
pnpm --filter web build pnpm --filter infra exec cdk deploy shop-sbx-<name>-api -c env=sbx -c owner=<name> -c senderEmail=<your email> Figure 03. The identity shown as Verified in SES.
5.4.3. Add to cart Goal: see that a signed-in customer’s cart is stored on the server, and that a guest cart is merged in at sign-in.
Open the web app signed out, open an in-stock product, click Thêm vào giỏ (Add to cart). The guest cart lives in the browser (localStorage). Sign in. The web app calls POST /api/v1/cart/merge (with an Idempotency-Key) to merge the guest cart into the account cart, then clears the guest cart. Add another product and open Giỏ hàng (Cart). Figure 04. Cart page with 2 products, signed in.
Check: Console → DynamoDB → the ...CartsTable... table of shop-sbx-<name>-api → Explore items. There is one item whose userId is your Cognito sub, with an items list of { productId, quantity, addedPrice, addedAt } and a version.
Figure 05. The cart item in the carts table.
5.4.4. Place an order Goal: create an order and see what one DynamoDB transaction writes.
In the cart, tick 1 product (leave the other), click Đặt hàng (Place order). The checkout page shows the chosen item and free shipping. Fill in name, phone, address and province (fake data), click Xác nhận đặt hàng (Confirm order). The web app opens the order detail page. The status starts as “Chờ xác nhận” (PENDING); reload a few seconds later and it shows “Đã xác nhận” (CONFIRMED), set by the worker. Figure 06. The checkout page before confirming (fake data).
Figure 07. The order detail page showing “Đã xác nhận”.
Check in DynamoDB:
...OrdersTable... → Explore items, filter userId = your sub. There are three kinds of items: the order (orderId is a ULID; status; items is a snapshot of name, price and quantity at order time; totalAmount; shippingAddress); the #OPEN counter with openOrders = 1 (open orders, at most 3); the #KEY#<Idempotency-Key> marker with refOrderId pointing at the order and expiresAt (24-hour TTL). ...ProductsTable...: the ordered product’s stock went down by exactly the quantity. ...CartsTable...: only the ordered item was removed from the cart; the unticked one is still there. All of these changes (decrementing stock, writing the order, removing the item from the cart, incrementing #OPEN, writing the marker) happen in one TransactWriteItems: either all of them happen or nothing changes. The stock decrement has the condition stock >= quantity, so when two customers buy the last unit at the same time only one succeeds; the other gets 409 OUT_OF_STOCK and stock never goes negative.
Figure 08. The three items in orders: the order, #OPEN, #KEY#….
5.4.5. Click twice, still one order (Idempotency-Key) Goal: send the same order request twice with the same Idempotency-Key and get exactly one order back.
The web app generates a UUID for each checkout and sends the same UUID again when the customer retries after a network error. Here we call the API directly to see it clearly.
Get an access token with the E2E app client (exists in sandbox, dev and staging only; never in prod). The password is read with read -s so it is not saved in your shell history:
API=<ApiUrl> CLIENT=<UserPoolE2eClientId> read -rp "Email: " EMAIL; read -rsp "Password: " PW; echo TOKEN=$(aws cognito-idp initiate-auth --region ap-southeast-1 --client-id "$CLIENT" \ --auth-flow USER_PASSWORD_AUTH --auth-parameters "USERNAME=$EMAIL,PASSWORD=$PW" \ --query AuthenticationResult.AccessToken --output text); unset PW Pick an in-stock product and its current price:
P=$(curl -s "$API/api/v1/products?limit=20" | jq -c '[.items[] | select(.stock > 0)][0] | {productId, price}') echo "$P" Build the request body and a key, then send it twice with the same key. The key command adds command so Git Bash does not run node through winpty (which fails when the output is captured into a variable):
KEY=$(command node -e "console.log(crypto.randomUUID())") BODY=$(jq -n --argjson p "$P" '{ items: [{ productId: $p.productId, quantity: 1, expectedPrice: $p.price }], shippingAddress: { fullName: "Test Customer", phone: "0912345678", address: "1 Test Street", province: "Ha Noi" } }') for i in 1 2; do curl -s -w '\n%{http_code}\n' -X POST "$API/api/v1/orders" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "Idempotency-Key: $KEY" -d "$BODY" | { read -r body; read -r code; echo "HTTP $code orderId=$(echo "$body" | jq -r .orderId)"; } done Expected: the first call returns HTTP 201, the second HTTP 200 with the same orderId. The orders table has only one new order; stock went down by 1 only.
Send the same key again but change quantity to 2: you get 422 with code IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED (same key, different content is a client error; no order is created).
BODY2=$(echo "$BODY" | jq '.items[0].quantity = 2') curl -s -w '\n%{http_code}\n' -X POST "$API/api/v1/orders" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "Idempotency-Key: $KEY" -d "$BODY2" | { read -r body; read -r code; echo "HTTP $code code=$(echo "$body" | jq -r .code)"; } Figure 09. The two calls (201 then 200, same orderId) and the different-content call (422).
How the server does it (ADR-0017, docs/business/ordering.md BR-04): Powertools Idempotency stores the result per key in order-idempotency for 24 hours; on top of that, the #KEY#… marker is written in the same transaction as the order, so even if the Lambda is cut off right after the transaction succeeds, a retry still finds the existing order instead of creating a new one.
You just created a real order in your sandbox. Cancel it in section 5.4.9 or on the web app (/orders) to restock. Each account can have at most 3 open orders; a 4th gets 409 TOO_MANY_OPEN_ORDERS.
5.4.6. A changed price creates no order Goal: see that the server does not trust the price sent by the client.
Resend the request from section 5.4.5 with a wrong expectedPrice and a new key:
KEY=$(command node -e "console.log(crypto.randomUUID())") BAD=$(echo "$BODY" | jq '.items[0].expectedPrice -= 1000') curl -s -X POST "$API/api/v1/orders" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Idempotency-Key: $KEY" -d "$BAD" | jq Expected: 409, code is PRICE_CHANGED, and changedItems has expectedPrice (what you sent) and currentPrice (the real price). No new order, stock unchanged. On the web app, the checkout page shows the new price so the customer can review and confirm again.
Figure 10. The 409 PRICE_CHANGED response.
Other business errors of POST /api/v1/orders (all application/problem+json):
Code When OUT_OF_STOCK (409) An item lacks stock or is no longer sold, with invalidItems TOO_MANY_OPEN_ORDERS (409) The account already has 3 PENDING/CONFIRMED orders ORDER_IN_PROGRESS (409) The previous call with the same key has not finished; retry with the same key after a few seconds IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED (422) Same key, different content (400) Missing Idempotency-Key or invalid body 5.4.7. No lost orders when the worker stops Goal: see SQS keep an order while the worker is paused, and the worker continue when resumed.
The API only writes the PENDING order and pushes { orderId, userId, type: "PLACED", correlationId } to the queue (type is CANCELLED for a cancelled order); the customer gets a response right away without waiting for the email. The worker does the rest later.
Console → Lambda → function shop-sbx-<name>-api-OrderProcessorFunction… → Configuration → Triggers → select the SQS trigger → Edit → untick Activate trigger → Save. Place an order on the web app. The order detail page stays at “Chờ xác nhận”, even after reloading. Console → SQS → queue …-OrdersQueue… → Send and receive messages → Poll for messages. Open the message: the body has only orderId, userId, type (PLACED), correlationId, no address or phone number; correlationId is also in the Attributes tab (a message attribute). Note: polling hides the message for 60 seconds (visibility timeout); do not click Delete. Turn the trigger back on (Activate trigger → Save). Within a minute the order shows “Đã xác nhận” and the confirmation email arrives. Figure 11. The SQS trigger shown as Disabled.
Figure 12. The message in the orders queue while the worker is off.
Figure 13. The order switching to “Đã xác nhận” after the trigger is back on.
Check the worker log: CloudWatch → Logs Insights, log group …-OrderProcessorLogs…:
fields @timestamp, level, message, orderId | filter correlationId = "<correlationId from the message in section 5.4.5>" | sort @timestamp asc The correlationId flows from the API to the worker; the log has no email, phone number or address.
Figure 14. The worker’s Logs Insights result.
If one message fails 3 times in a row (e.g. a wrong IAM permission, an SNS error), SQS moves it to …-OrdersDeadLetterQueue… and the order stays PENDING, not lost. Step-by-step handling is in docs/runbooks/dlq-orders.md. In prod, the orders-dlq alarm fires when the DLQ has a message.
5.4.8. The confirmation email is sent exactly once Goal: see the confirmation email and the duplicate-send protection.
Open the inbox of the verified address: there is a confirmation email with the order ID, name × quantity, total, cash on delivery, free shipping. It deliberately has no name, address, phone number or link. ...OrderIdempotencyTable... table → Explore items: there is a new item whose id starts with the worker function name (…OrderProcessorFunction…), with status = COMPLETED and expiration (24 hours later). The email’s dedup key is the userId plus <orderId>#CONFIRMED; Powertools stores the key as a hash, so the order ID is not readable in id. SQS delivers “at least once”, so the worker may receive the same message twice; the second time it finds this COMPLETED record and does not send the email again. Figure 15. The order confirmation email.
Figure 16. The worker’s item in order-idempotency (id starting with …OrderProcessorFunction…, status = COMPLETED).
The worker works in this order (docs/business/ordering.md, SQS flow):
Change PENDING → CONFIRMED with a conditional write status = PENDING (skipped if the order was cancelled). Publish order-confirmed to SNS (only orderId, userId, confirmation time, productId and quantity) so the recommendation module records the purchase. Send the email through SES, deduplicated by Powertools Idempotency. If SES rejects the email (e.g. the recipient is not verified in the sandbox), the worker logs a warning and the OrderEmailRejected metric, does not retry and does not send the message to the DLQ: the order is still confirmed normally.
5.4.9. Cancel an order, restock exactly once Goal: see cancelling restock in the same transaction, and never twice.
Web app → Đơn hàng (Orders) → open an order in “Đã xác nhận” → Huỷ đơn (Cancel order) → confirm in the dialog.
The order shows “Đã huỷ” (Cancelled). A few seconds later a cancellation email arrives (sent by the worker, dedup key <orderId>#CANCELLED).
Check: the product’s stock in products was added back; openOrders in the #OPEN item went down by 1.
Cancel again through the API:
curl -s -X DELETE "$API/api/v1/orders/<orderId>" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq It returns 409 with code CANNOT_CANCEL; stock is not added back a second time (the cancel transaction is conditional on the current status).
Figure 17. The cancelled order detail page.
Figure 18. The cancellation email.
Figure 19. The 409 CANNOT_CANCEL response on the second cancel.
5.4.10. Admin moves the order through delivery Goal: use an admin account to move an order CONFIRMED → SHIPPED → DELIVERED.
Add your account to the admin group (the group already exists in the user pool):
aws cognito-idp admin-add-user-to-group --region ap-southeast-1 \ --user-pool-id <UserPoolId> --username <your email> --group-name admin If the command returns UserNotFoundException, pass your userId (the account’s sub) to --username instead of the email.
Sign out and sign back in on the web app so the new token carries the admin group. The account menu now shows “Trang quản trị” (Admin page).
Open /admin. Admin accounts must turn on two-factor authentication: if it is off, the web app sends you to the setup page; follow it (scan the QR code with an authenticator app), then return to /admin.
Place a new order (with a normal account or this one) and wait for “Đã xác nhận”.
Tab Chờ giao (Awaiting shipment) → Chuyển sang Đang giao (Move to shipping) → confirm. The order moves to the Đang giao tab; openOrders goes down by 1 (the goods have left the warehouse, so the customer can order again).
Tab Đang giao → Đã giao (Delivered). The customer’s order page shows “Đã giao”.
Figure 20. The /admin page, Awaiting shipment tab, with the newly confirmed order.
Figure 21. The confirmation dialog for moving to shipping.
Figure 22. The customer’s order detail page showing “Đã giao”.
Check the permission: call the admin API with the token of an account not in the admin group:
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" "$API/api/v1/admin/orders?status=CONFIRMED" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN_CUSTOMER" It returns 403. Without a token, 401. The permission is checked in the backend from the groups in the JWT, not by whether the web app shows a button.
5.4.11. Cost of this part Measured on the author’s sandbox account, running the lab from 22 to 24/11/2026: Cost Explorer (Credits excluded) shows 0 USD for every service, within the free tier. Running the lab for a few hours and then deleting it costs almost nothing; if you leave the stacks running for long, check Billing again.
Service Use in this part Measured in the lab Lambda ordering, order-processor, admin A few dozen invocations in the lab $0 (within the free tier) DynamoDB carts, orders, order-idempotency On-demand, a few hundred reads and writes; orders has point-in-time recovery $0 (within the free tier) SQS orders queue and DLQ A few dozen messages $0 (within the free tier) SES A few emails (sandbox) $0 (within the free tier) SNS order-confirmed A few messages $0 (within the free tier) Figure 23. Cost Explorer, Group by: Service as in 5.2.
Figure 23b. Free plan page: the account is still on the free plan.
5.4.12. Clean up All sales-flow resources (tables carts, orders, order-idempotency, the orders queue and its DLQ, the three Lambdas, log groups, the admin group in the user pool) belong to the shop-sbx-<name>-api stack and are deleted with it, so follow 5.7 Clean up.
Two things are outside the stack and must be removed separately:
The SES identity created with the CLI:
aws sesv2 delete-email-identity --email-identity <your email> --region ap-southeast-1 The “Black Magic” entry in your phone’s authenticator app (if you turned on two-factor authentication in section 5.4.10).
Check Billing the next day as in 5.7.

title: Events Participated
content:
During the internship I attended 3 events, all held at the AWS Vietnam office in the Bitexco tower (Ho Chi Minh City).
# Event Date Role 1 FCAJ Buildrathon 2026 Kickoff and the talkshow “The Thinking Behind Building The Bot” (CMC Global) 26/09/2026 Attendee 2 AWS Cloud & AI Day 2026 29/09/2026 Attendee 3 Fireside Chat with Dr. Werner Vogels 02/10/2026 Attendee Event 1: FCAJ Buildrathon 2026 Kickoff and the talkshow “The Thinking Behind Building The Bot” Date: 26/09/2026 Location: AWS Vietnam office, Bitexco, Ho Chi Minh City Role: attendee Partner: CMC Global Main content:
An introduction to the First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) program: why it exists, the internship milestones and how teams build their final projects. The talkshow “The Thinking Behind Building The Bot” with CMC Global: Practical AI Agent thinking: from laying the architecture foundation for a bot to optimizing AI Agents in an enterprise setting. Solving the challenges: dissecting hard test cases live with the experts, learning through real problems. Career connections: 1-1 conversations with the CMC Global HR team at the event. Reflections and lessons:
This was one of the first times I clearly understood what FCAJ is and why it was created: not only learning AWS services but building a real product as a team, with a company-like process. The talkshow showed me that building a bot or an AI Agent does not start with calling a model but with the architecture: where the data comes from, how input is controlled, how it behaves on failure. I carried this into how our team designed shop-ai’s recommendations: behaviour data is hashed before storage, and results are only switched on after passing a quality gate. Talking directly with HR helped me understand what companies expect from a new cloud engineer. Event 2: AWS Cloud & AI Day 2026 Date: 29/09/2026 Location: AWS Vietnam office, Bitexco, Ho Chi Minh City Role: attendee Main content:
The biggest AWS event I attended during the internship, with discussions and live, hands-on breakdowns of real cloud and AI problems. A live link with the Hanoi venue, so attendees in Ho Chi Minh City could follow the Hanoi sessions as well. A meeting place for the Builder community to share experience learning and building on AWS. Reflections and lessons:
The practical breakdowns showed me how working engineers choose services: they always start from the problem, the cost and the operations, not from the technology. Our team applied this when choosing a serverless architecture for shop-ai and estimating costs with the AWS Pricing Calculator from the start. Meeting other Builders gave me motivation, and I learned how other teams split work, write documentation and review code. I realized the community is part of learning: ask in the right place, and share back what you have built (for example through blog posts in the AWS Study Group). Event 3: Fireside Chat with Dr. Werner Vogels Date: 02/10/2026 Location: AWS Vietnam office, Bitexco, Ho Chi Minh City Role: attendee Speaker: Dr. Werner Vogels, CTO of Amazon Main content (also checked against the summary The Invariable Lessons of Tech and Humanity by Le Vu Xuan An on AWS Builder Center):
Build it yourself when off-the-shelf software cannot scale: the story of Amazon’s database outage at peak season, which led to the technology behind DynamoDB. Most real access is key-value reads and writes that do not need a relational database. Measure tail latency: the median hides the worst customer experience; measure at very high percentiles such as P99.9. “Everything fails all the time”: design so that losing one or two data centers does not stop the service, and rehearse for real with GameDays so recovery is automatic, not manual. Pay-as-you-go: puts the burden on the provider, who must keep serving well to keep customers. The “Renaissance Developer” in the AI era: curiosity and continuous learning, systems thinking, ownership of the outcome, broad knowledge, good communication. Ownership stays with the engineer: AI writing code is like an imprecise natural-language compiler, so production bugs, security flaws and architecture remain the engineer’s job; humans keep judgment, creativity and empathy. Avoid complacency: the talk closed with a reminder not to do something just because “we’ve always done it this way”. Reflections and lessons:
Hearing Amazon’s CTO in person was the most memorable experience of the internship. His points are very close to what our team does: Design for failure: shop-ai orders go through an SQS queue with a DLQ, so a failing worker does not lose orders. Rehearse for real: the team rehearsed restoring a DynamoDB table with PITR on staging, and deliberately broke the session-revoke trigger to see how the system reacts. Measure the tail: the team measures p95 in k6 load tests instead of just the average; after this talk I understood why large systems go even higher. Own AI-written code: the team uses AI assistance, but every change goes through review, tests and a check against the real code before merging. The “Renaissance Developer” idea made me rethink how I learn: not just one service, but how systems fit together and how to talk with business people about cost and risk.

title: Recommendations and Data Security
content:
This chapter walks you through rebuilding the recommendation part of shop-ai: generating data and evaluating the models locally, running the nightly recommendation pipeline on AWS, checking that user data is anonymized, and running a recommendation poisoning experiment. Finish 5.1 Introduction, 5.2 Prerequisite and 5.3 Infrastructure first: the sandbox stack shop-sbx-<name> must be deployed to your account. In this chapter <name> is the name you used in -c owner=<name> when deploying.
Objectives After this chapter you will:
Understand why the team built its own recommendation models on Lambda + DynamoDB instead of Amazon Personalize (ADR-0016). Run two recommendation models locally and compare them with a bestseller baseline using precision@10 and coverage. Run the nightly recommendation job on AWS manually, read its log, inspect the recs table and call the recommendation API. Confirm that the events table holds no real user IDs (HMAC). Measure the impact of fake accounts spamming events, before and after the defenses. 5.5.1. Recommendation architecture Figure 00. Recommendation diagram with numbered flows 1–6: (1) the web calls the API through CloudFront; (2) VIEW, ADD_TO_CART events are stored with the user id hashed by the HMAC key from SSM; (3) PURCHASE events come from SNS order-confirmed (chapter 5.4) through SQS; (4) at 02:00 every night EventBridge Scheduler runs recs-pipeline, which reads events and products, writes a new version to recs and activates it only when it beats the baseline; (5) the recs Lambda serves the ACTIVE version; (6) CloudWatch alarms when the job has not succeeded (prod). Open the interactive diagram, drawn with the AWSketch skill from a JSON spec. This part is also steps 10–11 of the shared architecture diagram in 5.1.
Recommendation type Method Data used Frequently bought together Association rules (support, confidence, lift) from orders PURCHASE only For you Item-based collaborative filtering, cosine similarity VIEW (1), ADD_TO_CART (3), PURCHASE (5); each user–product pair takes the highest weight Bestsellers (baseline, new users) Count orders over 30 days, fall back to 90 then 365 days if too few, then newest products PURCHASE Each night the pipeline writes a new version to the recs table, and only then switches the ACTIVE pointer. Re-running on the same day does not duplicate data; a version that scores worse than the baseline on the last 30 days is not activated.
5.5.2. Preparation Completed 5.2 Prerequisite: AWS CLI, Node, pnpm, the shop-ai repo cloned, the HMAC key /shop/sbx/events/hmac-key created (the key step is in 5.2; without it purchase events fail with ParameterNotFound and go to the DLQ). Completed 5.3: the shop-sbx-<name> stack is deployed. Python 3.13 or later and uv (uv installs the right version from data/.python-version; Python 3.14 is only the Lambda runtime). An account registered on your web app (URL in the WebUrl output of the web stack). cd shop-ai/data uv sync uv run pytest # environment check, everything must pass 5.5.3. Generate data and evaluate models locally Generate synthetic data The generator creates 600 users in 4 groups (gamers, office workers, programming students, designers), buying by built-in patterns (e.g. graphics cards are often bought with power supplies), spread over 365 days, on the web app’s 102 products on sale (the seed in 5.3 loads 104 products; the 2 discontinued ones are left out of the data).
uv run data --out generated --seed 42 The folder has 7 files: users.csv, products.csv, orders.csv, order_items.csv, cart_items.csv, interactions_train.csv, interactions_test.csv.
Evaluate Train and test sets are split by time (the last 30 days are the test set), the same way the pipeline scores a new version before activating it.
uv run data-eval --data generated # Frequently bought together vs baseline uv run data-eval-for-you --data generated # For you vs baseline Results over 4 seeds (details in docs/business/recommendation.md section 4.1):
Baseline precision@10 Model precision@10 Baseline coverage Model coverage Frequently bought together (rules, baseline when no rule) 0.029–0.037 0.048–0.058 0.108 0.618–0.667 For you 0.029–0.044 0.047–0.054 0.137–0.177 0.833–0.873 The screenshot below is seed 42: the “Luật mua kèm” row (0.0448) is the rules alone; the table above uses the “rules, baseline when no rule” row (0.0485) because that is how the pipeline really runs.
Reading the numbers: the synthetic data has built-in buying patterns, so the results show that the pipeline and models learn those patterns correctly, not yet that the models do better with real customers.
5.5.4. Run the recommendation pipeline on AWS The pipeline is deployed with the API stack (infra/lib/recs-pipeline.ts): a Python 3.14 Lambda that runs at 02:00 Vietnam time through EventBridge Scheduler, retrying twice on failure. In sandbox, dev and staging the job mixes in synthetic data because there are almost no real buyers; prod uses only real events (SYNTHETIC=0).
Check the schedule Console → EventBridge → Schedules, open the ...RecsPipelineNightly... schedule of stack shop-sbx-<name>-api. Check the expression cron(0 2 * * ? *), time zone Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh, target Lambda ...RecsPipeline..., 2 retries. Run it manually once Console → Lambda, open function shop-sbx-<name>-api-RecsPipeline.... Test tab → Create new event, name manual, content {} → Test. Expected result: green “succeeded” box, about 4 seconds, about 100 MB of memory used. Read the log Each run prints exactly one JSON line, with counts and scores only, no user IDs. Open the Monitor tab → View CloudWatch logs, or use Logs Insights:
fields @timestamp, products, realEvents, syntheticEvents, gates.ALSO_BOUGHT.model.precision, gates.ALSO_BOUGHT.baseline.precision | filter message = "Job gợi ý mỗi đêm xong" | sort @timestamp desc | limit 5 (The log message is in Vietnamese in the code; keep the filter as is.)
Expected: gates only has ALSO_BOUGHT and FOR_YOU, each with a model score above the baseline. BESTSELLER is the baseline itself, so it has no gate and is always activated. results shows activated: true for ALSO_BOUGHT and BESTSELLER. FOR_YOU is only written for real users (with a userIdHash in the events table), so it may write 0 rows if you have not done the anonymization step below yet. Do that step, then run the job manually again to see rows for FOR_YOU.
Inspect the recs table and call the API Console → DynamoDB → the ...Recs... table of stack shop-sbx-<name>-api → Explore items, find pk = META: there are 3 pointers ACTIVE#ALSO_BOUGHT, ACTIVE#FOR_YOU, ACTIVE#BESTSELLER, each with activeVersion set to the run date. In a browser: <WebUrl>/api/v1/recs/bestsellers?limit=3. Expected: "source":"BESTSELLER" and 3 products. Open a laptop’s detail page on your web app: the “Frequently bought together” block shows a laptop sleeve, a mouse and an HDMI cable. Alert when the job stops running (prod) Prod has an alarm recs-pipeline-no-success: it fires when there is no successful run for 26 hours in a row (hours with no data count as failures, to also catch the case where the schedule does not invoke the Lambda). On the first deploy the alarm fires right away because there has been no run yet; one manual run brings it back to OK. How to handle it is in docs/runbooks/recs-pipeline.md.
5.5.5. Anonymizing user data The events table is the model’s input data. It does not store real user IDs: the events Lambda takes userId from the JWT (it does not trust data sent by the client) and stores userIdHash = HMAC-SHA256(key, userId). The HMAC key is in SSM Parameter Store as a SecureString (/shop/<env>/events/hmac-key, created in 5.2), not in the repo or the template. So anyone who can read the events table or the training data files still cannot tell who an event belongs to.
Sign in to your web app, open a product detail page, click Add to cart (the button label is in Vietnamese on the site: Thêm vào giỏ). Note the time. Console → DynamoDB → the ...Events... table of stack shop-sbx-<name>-api → Explore items, sort by time. Check the two new rows VIEW and ADD_TO_CART: userIdHash is a 64-character hex string, with no email or original userId; there is a ttl of 90 days. Try sending an event while signed out, or sending PURCHASE from the client: the API returns 401 and 400. PURCHASE is written only by the system once an order is confirmed (SNS order-confirmed → SQS → Lambda), exactly once per product in the order. 5.5.6. Recommendation poisoning experiment An attacker creates many fake accounts and spams views and add-to-carts for a rarely bought product to push it into real users’ recommendations. The experiment runs on synthetic data and computes recommendations exactly as the pipeline does.
cd shop-ai/data uv run data-poison --seed 42 How events of one user–product pair are combined 50 accounts × 50 repeats: % of real users who see the target product sum: add up every action (the common approach) 38.8%–43.2% max: take the highest weight (what the pipeline uses) 0.3%–2.0% (no attack: 0%–3.3%) Three layers of defense:
Combine with max: repeating an action does not raise the score, so repeated spam has no effect. “Frequently bought together” learns only from real PURCHASE events: the client cannot send PURCHASE, so this type is not affected. WAF in prod: a limit of 300 /api/v1/events requests per 5 minutes per IP, plus IP reputation and the core rule set (infra/lib/waf-stack.ts, details in 5.3). The sandbox has no WAF, so this layer can only be checked on the team’s prod. Known limitation: calling the API Gateway URL directly (bypassing CloudFront) skips WAF; API Gateway throttling and the max layer still apply (threat model C1).
5.5.7. Cost of this part Estimate for one environment, prices for ap-southeast-1 and us-east-1 (WAF), November 2026:
Service Usage Estimate per month Pipeline Lambda Once a night, about 4 seconds, 512 MB Almost $0 (within Free Tier) DynamoDB recs About 2,200 writes a night, on-demand, ttl removes old versions Under $0.10 DynamoDB events A few thousand events, ttl 90 days Under $0.10 EventBridge Scheduler 30 invocations $0 (Free Tier) WAF (prod only) 1 web ACL, 5 rules About $10 + $0.60 per million requests Comparison: Amazon Personalize charges per training hour and per recommendation request, which can cause bill shock during demos; this is why the mentor suggested building our own (ADR-0016).
5.5.8. Clean up The recommendation part lives only in the API stack (shop-sbx-<name>-api): the pipeline Lambda, the EventBridge schedule, the events and recs tables and the log groups are all deleted with the stack in the sandbox, so follow 5.7 Clean up with no extra step. The HMAC key /shop/sbx/events/hmac-key belongs to no stack; delete it as in 5.7.3, and check Billing the next day as in 5.7.
Note for the team’s prod environment (not needed for the lab): the prod events and recs tables are retained when the stack is deleted (RETAIN), and events also has deletion protection; prod WAF (about $10/month) is cleaned up following docs/runbooks/waf.md, section “Dọn sau khi nộp bài” (cleanup after submission).
